questions.q: A play's last scene gathers all the separated characters for a wedding feast, but one humiliated character storms off vowing revenge. What does the classical division say about this ending?
choices: It's a tragedy, because someone is left unhappy
It's a comedy whose inclusion has a limit: the group is rebuilt, but someone is left outside
It's a problem play, because it contains a wedding
It's satire, because nobody is redeemed
questions.explain: Comedy moves toward inclusion and reunion; the excluded figure, like Malvolio in Twelfth Night, shows the edge of that community.

questions.q: A writer's drama brings its hero to the brink of execution, then a pardon arrives and no one dies. Under John Fletcher's definition, what is it?
choices: A tragedy, because the stakes were mortal
A comedy, because it ends happily
A tragicomedy: it brings characters near death but has no deaths
A melodrama, because the pardon is a deus ex machina
questions.explain: Fletcher: no deaths keeps it from tragedy, bringing some near death keeps it from comedy.

questions.q: Which plays did F. S. Boas group as Shakespeare's "problem plays" in 1896?
choices: The Tempest, The Winter's Tale, Cymbeline and Pericles
Richard II, Henry IV and Henry V
Titus Andronicus, Timon of Athens and Coriolanus
All's Well That Ends Well, Measure for Measure, Troilus and Cressida and Hamlet
questions.explain: Boas borrowed the term from the Ibsen-era problem play for works whose endings don't settle the moral questions they raise. The late plays are the "romances".

questions.q: Chekhov called The Cherry Orchard a comedy; Stanislavski staged it as a tragedy. What does this dispute show about modern tragicomedy?
choices: That Chekhov misunderstood his own play
That modern tragicomedy is often a doubleness of tone rather than a plot that swerves from death
That comedy must end in a marriage
That a play's genre is fixed by its subtitle
questions.explain: Both readings are in the text; the uncertainty whether to laugh or grieve is the form.

questions.q: Bong Joon-ho's Parasite switches from con-artist comedy to violence at a birthday party. Why does the switch feel earned rather than a broken promise?
choices: Because the comedy was already about the thing that turns violent: class
Because tragedy always follows comedy in Frye's cycle
Because the audience was told in advance by a narrator
Because a death keeps it from being tragicomedy
questions.explain: A blended form keeps its contract when the tonal turn grows out of what the comedy was about all along.

questions.q: What does a comedy fundamentally promise its audience?
choices: That the hero will be destroyed by a flaw
That we'll understand why a loss had to happen
That the trouble will be survived and the group put back together
That every institution will fail
questions.explain: Comedy promises survival and reunion; tragedy promises meaningful loss; irony and satire show a world without effective heroes.

questions.q: Who first used the word tragicomoedia, and why?
choices: Aristotle, in the Poetics, for Euripides' happy endings
Plautus, in the prologue to Amphitryon, for a play mixing gods and kings with slaves and jokes
Philip Sidney, to praise mixed plays
Guarini, as a title for Il pastor fido
questions.explain: Plautus coined it; Sidney later scorned "mongrel tragi-comedy" and Guarini defended the form.

ideas: Comedy moves toward inclusion, rebuilding a community; tragedy moves toward isolation, cutting one person off.
The classical rule of thumb: comedy ends in marriage or reunion, tragedy in death or separation.
A tragicomedy has no deaths, which keeps it from tragedy, yet brings characters near death, which keeps it from comedy.
Each form is a contract: break the promise the opening made without reason and the audience feels cheated.
